claim: The dictionary×text citation matrix has a core–periphery (nested) topology — each dictionary's cited texts are approximately a subset of the next-broader dictionary's — rather than falling into disjoint tradition communities (modular).
method: Binarise the dict×text citation matrix; compute NODF nestedness (Almeida-Neto et al. 2008) and Barber (2007) bipartite modularity Q (label propagation, LPAwb+ core, best of 6 restarts). Compare each to 1000 degree-preserving (fixed-fixed) permutation nulls generated by trial-swap randomisation; permutation p = (#null >= observed + 1)/(nNull + 1), per the Dror et al. (2018) protocol.
interpretation: PH1 CANON-CORE is not supported — the matrix is less nested than a one-canon random draw with the same margins and more modular than it: it is significantly MODULAR (Barber Q 0.4757 vs degree-preserving null mean 0.4094, permutation p 0.001) and is if anything LESS nested than chance (NODF 26.857 vs null mean 31.356, p 1). The cited canon is NOT one additive core–periphery ladder: the assignments cluster beyond what a one-canon draw with the same breadths and popularities forces. The partition the optimiser finds is two key-sharing pairs (ap+ap90, pwkvn+sch) plus singletons — a shared resolver key is sufficient for both pairs — and the margin over the null survives variant folding (H5295 ledger). A50 §4 reports the margin, the partition and that alternative; tradition names come from the curated map, not from the partition.

The matrix is extremely sparse and long-tailed: 567 of the 874 cited node labels are private to a single dictionary and on the committed labels none is shared by all 11 <ls>-tagged dicts (the broadest by reach, Rāmāyaṇa, appears in 9; the Ṛgveda reaches all 11 once its Rigveda spelling is folded, and four texts reach every dictionary with a usable yield — H5295). A thin universal head (Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata, Ṛgveda) doubles as a shared reading list, but the mass of each apparatus is its own idiosyncratic tail; private labels inflate raw Q in observed and null alike, and the margin over the null is what carries the modular signal.
limitations: MW contributes only its 5 bibliographic <ls> markers here — 63,582 grammatical/editorial <ls> markers were filtered as non-text (audit: data/citations/ls_citation_nontext_filtered.tsv) — so MW's apparatus is under-represented relative to its true citation load.
Coverage is <ls>-tagged citations only; prose/iti citations (VCP, SKD, WIL) are not in the graph, so those dictionaries' rows understate their real canon.
Nestedness/modularity are computed on presence/absence; citation COUNT weighting is shown in the heatmap but not folded into the topology statistics.

Degree-preserving nulls hold each dictionary's breadth and each text's popularity fixed; the test asks only whether the ARRANGEMENT of citations is more nested / more modular than that constraint forces.

Barber Q is a heuristic (label-propagation, best of 6 restarts) not an exhaustive optimum, so the reported Q is a lower bound; the observed-vs-null comparison assumes the optimiser reaches comparable quality on both, and the null distribution's very small spread makes the exact p sensitive — read the direction (modular, not nested), not the third decimal of p.
boundary: Derived from two committed atlas citation TSVs only; no source/corpus read, no public-facing decision, no external maker work. Owner repo csl-atlas.
